title: Daguerreotype and Early Photography
welcome_lead: 1839: Daguerre announces a process that captures light on silvered copper.
meta_desc: A-Level Art & Design: Daguerreotype, calotype, and the birth of photography.

concepts.def: Daguerre's 1839 silver-iodide photographic process on copper.

walkthroughs.body_html: On 19 August 1839, the French government announced the Daguerreotype process, freely offered to the world (Britain excepted by patent). Photography became public.
In 1841, Henry Fox Talbot patented the calotype — a paper negative permitting multiple positive prints. The negative-positive system, not Daguerre's silver plate, became photography's future.
In 1878, Eadweard Muybridge photographed Leland Stanford's galloping horse with twelve cameras at Palo Alto — proving all four hooves leave the ground simultaneously and anticipating cinema.

mcqs.q: Muybridge's galloping-horse study was made in:
Was the daguerreotype a negative-positive process?
options: No — daguerreotypes were painted entirely by hand.
No — photography was banned from galleries until 1990.
Yes — all early photography used negatives.
No — it produced a single unique image on a silvered plate; Talbot's calotype introduced the negative for multiple prints.

mcqs.q: What did Muybridge's motion studies of a galloping horse show?
options: They proved a horse always keeps one hoof on the ground.
They proved cameras cannot capture motion.
Sequential photographs proved that all four hooves leave the ground mid-gallop.
No — daguerreotypes were painted entirely by hand.

mcqs.q: Was photography immediately accepted as an art form?
options: Yes — galleries embraced photography as art from 1839.
No — photography was banned from galleries until 1990.
No — it was long dismissed as mechanical record, and movements like Pictorialism campaigned for its artistic status.
No — daguerreotypes were painted entirely by hand.
